title: Conditional Statements
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of conditional statements and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.

content.intro: Conditional Statements is part of Conditions, Loops, and Control Flow. Start with introduction to if and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: An if condition is expected to be a single non-missing logical value; vector conditions need a vectorized tool.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: An if condition is expected to be a single non-missing logical value; vector conditions need a vectorized tool. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Test a condition at the boundary and decide how NA should be handled. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For conditional statements, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
